title: Middle of the Linked List
description: Brute force to optimized: counting the length first versus a single-pass slow/fast pointer technique.

blocks.text: Given the head of a singly linked list, return the middle node of the linked list. If there are two middle nodes (an even number of nodes), return the SECOND middle node.

blocks.caption: A fast pointer moving twice as fast as a slow pointer reaches the end exactly when slow reaches the middle

blocks.text: Given the head of a linked list, find its middle node in a single pass, without first walking through to count the total number of nodes.

blocks.title: Analogy: Two Hikers on the Same Trail, One Twice as Fast
blocks.text: Like sending two hikers down the same trail at the same time, one walking at normal pace and the other jogging at exactly twice that pace. By the time the faster hiker reaches the end of the trail, the slower hiker, having covered exactly half the total distance, must be standing right at the trail's midpoint.

blocks.caption: Fast always covers exactly double the distance slow does, landing slow precisely at the midpoint

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["A list of 5 nodes has a single, unambiguous middle: the 3rd node","Middle node: 3","With an odd number of nodes, there's exactly one middle position"],["Answer","[3,4,5]","The problem returns the node itself, so the rest of the list from that point onward is shown"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["A list of 6 nodes has two middle candidates (3rd and 4th); the SECOND one is required","Middle node: 4","The problem specifically asks for the second middle when there are two"],["Answer","[4,5,6]","Returning node 4 and everything after it"]]}

blocks.text: Before walking through the list once just to count its length, then walking through it again to reach the halfway point, notice that a single coordinated pass with two pointers at different speeds can find the middle directly.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If one pointer moves exactly twice as fast as another, starting from the same position, the faster pointer will always have covered exactly twice the distance of the slower one at any given moment.

Observation 2: This means that by the time the fast pointer reaches the END of the list, the slow pointer must have covered exactly HALF that distance, landing it precisely at the middle.

Observation 3: For an odd-length list, this naturally lands slow on the single true middle node. For an even-length list, this specific loop condition (checking fast AND fast.next both exist) naturally lands slow on the SECOND of the two middle nodes, matching the problem's required tie-breaking rule.

Observation 4: No separate length-counting pass is ever needed, since the fast pointer's progress toward the end IS the signal for when slow has reached the middle.

Recognizing that a 1:2 speed ratio between two pointers directly finds the halfway point in a single pass is the same fundamental insight behind Floyd's cycle detection, just applied here to find a MIDPOINT instead of detecting a cycle.
This is the classic slow/fast pointer technique, the same fundamental idea as Floyd's cycle detection, applied here to locate the middle of the list in a single pass.
First walk through the entire list once to count its length, then walk through it again to reach the halfway point.

items: Walk through the list once, counting the total number of nodes.
Walk through the list a second time, advancing exactly (length // 2) steps from the head to reach the correct middle node.

codes.python:
def middle_node(head):
    length = 0
    node = head
    while node:
        length += 1                                                        # first pass: count the total number of nodes
        node = node.next
    node = head
    for _ in range(length // 2):                                           # second pass: walk exactly halfway to reach the middle
        node = node.next
    return node


if __name__ == "__main__":
    head = ListNode(1, ListNode(2, ListNode(3, ListNode(4, ListNode(5)))))
    result = middle_node(head)
    values = []
    while result:
        values.append(result.val)
        result = result.next
    print(values)

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The first pass counts nodes without modifying anything, purely to determine the list's total length.
Integer division (length // 2) correctly identifies the SECOND middle node for even-length lists, matching the problem's requirement.
The second pass walks exactly that many steps from the head to land precisely on the correct middle node.

blocks.text: The list length is correctly counted, and the middle node is correctly reached by walking exactly halfway, so the answer is always accurate.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), across two separate passes through the list (though still linear overall).
Space: O(1) extra.

Limitation: requiring two separate passes through the list (one to count, one to walk halfway) ignores that a single coordinated pass, using two pointers moving at different speeds, can find the exact same middle node directly.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force needs two separate passes. Instead, use two pointers, slow and fast, both starting at head. Advance slow by 1 node and fast by 2 nodes at each step, as long as fast and fast.next both exist. The moment fast can no longer advance (having reached or passed the end), slow has landed exactly on the middle node, in a single combined pass.
Initialize slow and fast to head. While fast is not null and fast.next is not null, advance slow by 1 node and fast by 2 nodes. Return slow once the loop ends.
Advance a slow pointer by 1 and a fast pointer by 2 each step; slow lands on the middle exactly when fast reaches the end.

codes.python:
def middle_node(head):
    slow = head
    fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next                                                   # slow advances 1 node per step
        fast = fast.next.next                                              # fast advances 2 nodes per step
    return slow                                                            # once fast reaches the end, slow sits at the middle


if __name__ == "__main__":
    head = ListNode(1, ListNode(2, ListNode(3, ListNode(4, ListNode(5, ListNode(6))))))
    result = middle_node(head)
    values = []
    while result:
        values.append(result.val)
        result = result.next
    print(values)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single combined pass through the list.
Space: O(1) extra, using only the 2 pointer variables.

Since fast always covers exactly twice the number of nodes that slow does (moving 2 versus 1 per step, starting together), by the time fast has traversed the full length of the list, slow must have traversed exactly half that length, landing it precisely at the middle. The specific loop condition (checking both fast and fast.next) naturally produces the SECOND middle node for even-length lists, matching this problem's exact tie-breaking requirement, without any extra special-case logic needed.

items: Both pointers start at head, requiring no special initialization for short lists.
The loop condition (fast != null && fast.next != null) safely allows fast to advance by 2 without ever dereferencing a null pointer.
The function returns slow directly, since by the time the loop naturally ends, slow already holds the correct middle node.

items: Using a wrong loop condition (e.g., only checking fast != null, not fast.next != null), which can cause a null pointer dereference when advancing fast by 2.
Counting the list length first and then walking halfway in a separate pass, missing the opportunity to combine both into one single pass.
Getting the "which middle node for even length" tie-break backward, returning the first middle instead of the required second one.

items: Explicitly connect this technique to Linked List Cycle's Floyd's algorithm, since both rely on the exact same "fast covers twice the distance of slow" mechanism, just applied to different goals (finding a midpoint here, versus detecting a cycle there).

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Find the middle of a linked list in a single pass" points directly to the slow/fast pointer technique, moving at a 1:2 speed ratio.

items: How would you modify this to return the FIRST middle node instead, for even-length lists? Change the loop condition to stop one step earlier (e.g., checking fast.next and fast.next.next before advancing), shifting where slow ends up.

How would you find the middle of a list that might also contain a cycle? Floyd's cycle detection would need to run first to confirm no cycle exists (or determine its length), since a genuinely cyclic list has no well-defined "middle" in the traditional sense.

How would you delete the middle node instead of just finding it? Track one additional pointer (the node just before slow) as the traversal proceeds, so its next pointer can be adjusted to skip over the middle node once found.

The same slow/fast pointer mechanism as Linked List Cycle's Floyd's algorithm, applied here to locate a midpoint instead of detecting a loop; also a common building block within Palindrome Linked List and Sort List elsewhere in this category.

blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) time (two passes), O(1) space.
Optimized (slow/fast pointers): O(n) time (one pass), O(1) space.
